title: Night waking
hook: a practice for 3 am: breath, a name, a prayer
tomorrow: why would a prophet bargain fifty daily prayers down to five?

segments.voice: Last week ended on the last words, one line of trust kept word for word before sleep. But some nights, sleep doesn't stay.

The refrigerator hums, the phone says 3:07, and sleep isn't coming back. A boy named Samuel woke in the dark once, in the temple at Shiloh, at the hour the Bible marks this way: ere the lamp of God went out. Someone called his name. He jumped up and ran to the old priest Eli, whose eyes had grown dim, and said: Here am I; for thou calledst me. And Eli said: I called not; lie down again.
screen: `3:07 A.M.` → `ERE THE LAMP OF GOD WENT OUT.` → `SOMEONE CALLS HIS NAME.` → `I CALLED NOT; LIE DOWN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: It happens again, and again. Three times Samuel runs to Eli. The text says why he kept getting it wrong: Samuel did not yet know the LORD. The third time, the old man understands. Go, lie down, he says, and if he call thee, say: Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth. So Samuel lies down in the dark and waits. The call comes: Samuel, Samuel. And he answers, Speak; for thy servant heareth. Some readers notice he leaves out the word LORD, as if he's still not sure. He answers anyway. Jews and Christians both read this night at Shiloh, and one teaching they draw from it is this: prayer can be listening, not only talking. Samuel's first word, here am I, is hineni in Hebrew, the same answer Abraham and Moses give when they're called. And notice the night wasn't easy. What Samuel heard was hard news about Eli's own house, and in the morning he was afraid to tell him. At three a.m., what calls may only be worry. Samuel's way doesn't argue with it. It turns waking into listening: a breath, a name, one line, and then attention, until morning comes.
screen: `THREE TIMES TO ELI.` · `SPEAK; FOR THY SERVANT HEARETH.` · `HINENI: HERE I AM.` · `PRAYER THAT LISTENS.` · then, large: `FOR THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes as if it were three in the morning, and take one slow breath. Say your own name once, quietly, the way it was said to Samuel. Then, if you pray, his line: Speak; for thy servant heareth; if you don't, simply: here I am. Listen until the bell.
Night waking: a small practice for the hours when sleep leaves, a breath, a name and a listening line, the way Samuel answered in the dark.
Pocket this one: for the night, a breath, a name, and here I am. Rest well.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Samuel's night call in 1 Samuel 3; his answer, 'Speak; for thy servant heareth', is used as a short prayer of listening, and 'here am I' (hineni) as the answer to a call.
